prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B058) first, but I now think that was partly a reflection of my own field and my own lab's neighbourhood rather than the strongest case on the table. The optical lattice clock is the candidate on which the committee's scientific arguments converge: three first places and six top-three rankings, from members with very different backgrounds. The physics is a clean example of what I value. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift that would otherwise ruin a lattice clock, so many atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. This opened a regime of fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 that is reproduced by several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) and compared across links. It already delivers physics beyond metrology: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on drifting constants, dark-matter searches, and many-body effects inside the clock itself. Attribution is unusually clean for a two-person prize, with Katori as originator and first realiser and Ye as the group that pushed it to the accuracy frontier. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize are adjacent but do not cover this achievement, and the pending redefinition of the second shows the community regards it as settled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee may read this as a measurement-technology milestone that continues the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes rather than as a new discovery, and that the ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others) have claims the two names do not capture. The impact on the SI second is still prospective, because the redefinition has not yet happened. Against my own opening choice: B058 has only one first-place vote, mine, and I have an obvious bias and a possible conflict there. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits also makes a second superconducting-circuit award within two years hard to defend, and Wallraff is missing from the credited names.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranked B007 first because the magic-wavelength lattice cancels light shifts by design, giving atomic physics where theory and experiment agree to extraordinary precision, and she asked whether this is a new discovery or a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
responses.response: I agree with her physical judgement and think her own question can be answered. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions. The lattice clock is a different mechanism, in which a state-insensitive trap makes a large ensemble a quantum-limited oscillator. Its payoffs, redshift over millimetres and constraints on constants, are results about nature and not only about instruments. I would still ask her to be careful over credit. Her list of other contributors shows that the clean pair of Katori and Ye is a simplification, and the citation should say 'lattice clocks' and not 'optical clocks' in general, so that ion clocks stay outside it.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranked B007 first on the grounds that coherence, linewidth and systematic control are what turn spectroscopy into a measurement tool at 1e-18, and that repeated international clock comparisons show the result is stable. He flagged distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I think his experimental criterion is the right one and it favours B007, because the evidence is not one laboratory's record. It rests on repeated comparisons between independent clocks. I differ from him in one respect, which is his interest in matter-wave interferometry (B021) as a close second. That candidate has a harder credit problem, since Chu is excluded and Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich are disputed in the community, and it did not reach the shortlist. If he wants a second achievement in the same precision-measurement spirit, I would say B007 alone is more defensible than a split prize with it.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranked magic-angle graphene (B001) first, as a surprise in a material where theory and experiment form an unusually direct loop, and he ranked the lattice clock only fifth, noting possible perceived overlap with earlier metrology prizes.
responses.response: I take his point about the quality of the theory-experiment loop seriously and I ranked B001 third myself. My reservation is timing and settledness. The pairing mechanism is still unresolved, several correlated phases are debated, and the 2018 experimental credit is shared with Cao and the wider moire community, so the three-name allocation is contested. That is not fatal, and I would support B001 if the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize. But I would not call it more mature than the clock. I would ask him whether a citation limited to the prediction of flat bands and the observation of correlated states, without claiming the superconducting mechanism, would meet his concern, since that is the version I could defend.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig ranked B001 first because a simple analytical continuum model predicted the magic angle and was then tested directly by experiment, and he valued the clean mechanism and the field it opened. He ranked the lattice clock outside his top eight.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is exactly the kind of transparent theory that a good prize should reward. But the lattice clock has the same structure on a smaller scale: Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a simple, general mechanism, and it was tested to very high accuracy. His list was weighted toward statistical physics, which is a reason his view differs from the experimentalists' rather than evidence against B007. I would ask him to treat B001 as a strong alternative and to say whether the unresolved superconductivity and the credit to Cao and others make him prefer waiting a few years.

responses.point: Mark Pearce ranked IceCube (B039) first as a purpose-built instrument that opened a new observational window, and he ranked B007 second as a clear and timely measurement achievement.
responses.response: We agree that instrument-driven discoveries are the most convincing, and his second choice matches mine. On B039 I defer to him and Danielsson on astroparticle physics, but the credit problem looks harder there than for the clock. The collaboration has several hundred members, AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers complicate priority, and source identification is still evidence-level (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068). He himself notes the limited independent confirmation, since KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are still maturing. That makes it less settled than a clock result confirmed in many laboratories. I would be glad to see it prized later, but I do not think it should displace B007 now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the optical lattice clock as a discovery or as an instrument advance, given the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether the credit boundary with other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups can be defended with two names, and how to word the citation to keep it precise.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as supporting evidence of maturity or as an impact that has not yet been realised.
Whether circuit QED (B058) is a separate achievement from the 2025 prize, and whether Wallraff's omission from the credited names can be fixed within a three-person limit.
I am relying on my own recollection of the clock priority history and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: Specific conflict: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with Chalmers superconducting-circuit groups, and Chalmers hosted 2025 laureates Martinis and Clarke as WACQT guests. That is a clear connection to B058 (circuit QED), which I ranked first, and I should recuse myself from decisions on that candidate and treat my support for it as discounted. I also have a collaborative link to the dynamical-Casimir and giant-atom literature that is adjacent to it. No specific conflict is apparent for B007, B001, B008 or the other shortlisted candidates from the provided profile.
